title: Over half of surveyed migrants left villages to escape climate risks, RMMRU finds
excerpt: Most say life in the city is better, but many lack water, toilets and documents to get services. Researchers want migration treated as adaptation.

image.alt: Korail, Dhaka's largest informal settlement, seen from above beside Banani lake
image.credit: Aditya Kabir / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
About 53% of rural migrants surveyed in a new study moved to cities to escape climate-related risks, and about 25% moved for better jobs, The Business Standard reported. The findings were presented at a workshop in Chattogram on 2 November.

Main findings

  • Drivers of moving include smaller fish catches, failed harvests, lost assets, few rural jobs and the concentration of industry in Dhaka and Chattogram.
  • Families earned an average of Tk 7,446 a month before moving. Many now work in garments, transport, retail and day labour.
  • About 72% to 74% said their living standards improved, and nearly 75% were satisfied with their work.
  • Many lack safe water, toilets, waste collection, schooling and health care. In some areas 10 to 20 families share one toilet.
  • About 70% said the heat in the city was worse than at home.
  • Many cannot get government services because they lack birth registration or identity documents. Women reported age discrimination at work and no childcare.

What the researchers recommend

  • More rural jobs and agricultural support, so fewer people are forced to move.
  • New industry and satellite towns around Chattogram, including Anwara and Banshkhali.
  • Low-income migrants included in urban planning, with water, sanitation, housing, schooling, health care and social protection.
  • No denial of basic services to people without identity documents.
  • Migration treated as a form of climate adaptation, not “merely as a burden on cities”.

Why it matters

The study links two areas NGOs often handle separately: climate adaptation in coastal and rural districts, and urban poverty in informal settlements. Its finding that documents block access to services points to practical work: helping migrants register births and get ID so they can reach social protection. It is also relevant to Bangladesh’s case at COP31 that climate impacts already drive displacement.

Limitations

Workshop participants questioned the sample size and method and called for broader samples and more qualitative data. The coverage does not give the sample size or survey areas, and the satisfaction figures are self-reported.

Sources

  • Climate risks, livelihood crisis push rural people towards cities: Study, The Business Standard, 2 November 2026
